extracted.intended_audience: authors (novelists, memoirists, nonfiction/how-to writers) considering or preparing for a freelance manuscript evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on what a professional manuscript evaluation covers, how it differs from other levels of editing, what to expect in deliverables and pricing, and how to find/choose an appropriate editor. Focuses on novels, memoirs and how-to books (book-length manuscripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story advance appropriately? How are characters introduced and developed? How is the pacing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manuscript evaluation looks at structure as a big-picture lens; it may note problems but won’t do the hands-on restructuring a structural edit would. If structure is unclear or the manuscript isn’t cohesive, a developmental or structural edit may be more appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (stakes, goals, voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the stakes high enough? Is the story goal clear? Is the voice or perspective clear or strong? Does it earn each plot development? Does it require more suspense (or sensuality, or action)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations assess whether story elements (stakes, goals, voice) are working and whether plot developments are earned. They may recommend where to increase dramatic or sensory elements. This is treated at a high level rather than providing line-by-line rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics (grammar, word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there recurring grammatical issues? How effective are your word choices, including adjectives and adverbs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manuscript evaluation will note recurring mechanical problems but typically will not correct them for you (unlike copyediting/proofreading). It can flag patterns like overuse of passive voice or flat dialogue as examples to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For genre fiction, does the manuscript follow the accepted conventions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will check fit with genre expectations; failure to follow conventions may be raised as a barrier to acceptance/publishing. This is especially important when querying or submitting to genre markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of a manuscript evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A manuscript evaluation is a high-level analysis of your manuscript through multiple lenses and is much less detailed than a developmental edit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically delivered as an editorial letter running a few pages (usually no more than 10 pages); may include light markup to illustrate points. It gives a high-level overview of what works and what doesn’t and may refer authors to books/blogs/resources for deeper concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: How a manuscript evaluation differs from developmental/editing levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing is a deep-dive edit (multiple deep reads, hundreds of comments, rewrites, long editorial letters) while a manuscript evaluation is an overview and less expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have extensive notes, chapter drafts, or aren’t clear on your story, developmental editing is probably more appropriate. A developmental edit might include line rewrites and 30+ page editorial letters, whereas an evaluation will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverables and typical format (letter, markup, calls)
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluation typically includes an editorial letter (a few pages, often ≤10) and some editors include light markup; some offer an introductory call and a post-feedback discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors require a free 30-minute introductory call, include a 60-minute call post-feedback, and allow follow-up questions via email for a limited time. Level of feedback (breadth and depth) should be proportional to cost and clarified up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial manuscript evaluations and sample-page reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Some editors offer partial evaluations or review first 10–50 pages; a 5,000-word sample often reveals recurring writing issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short excerpts can show problems like passive voice or flat dialogue and give a sense of flow, but cannot reliably evaluate overall structure, plot, character arcs, themes, or full-manuscript story expressions because the editor lacks full context.

rubrics_metrics.name: What editors can and won’t do in an evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluation may mention recurring punctuation or other problems but will not correct them; it will address areas that pose problems for acceptance/publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect identification and diagnosis rather than comprehensive fixes. If hands-on line edits or corrections are needed, hire a copyeditor or line editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing expectations and billing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical fees: $300–$500 for a partial manuscript evaluation (20–25 double-spaced pages); $1,200–$1,500 for a full manuscript up to 60,000 words. Longer manuscripts often billed per-word after initial 60,000 or via stepped increases (example: $250 per additional 10,000 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of prices that seem too good to be true—proper evaluations take substantial time and expertise. Editors’ billing models vary (flat fee, per-word, stepped), so confirm what’s included. Ask for written proposals that specify deliverables.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to seek a manuscript evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally only when you’ve taken your manuscript as far as you can—an evaluation won’t be as useful if feedback covers revisions you already know you must make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have lots of notes or drafts and aren’t clear on the story, consider developmental editing first. Use an evaluation when the manuscript is cohesive enough that high-level feedback will be actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to find and choose the right editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask writers in your genre for recommendations; read editors’ blogs; look for editors experienced in your field (esp. academic books); request sample editorial letters or sample edits (with client permission); interview several editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain written proposals that detail exactly what the editor will do and deliver. Assess resonance with the editor’s communication style, experience, and worldview; a free intro call helps gauge fit. Don’t rely solely on editorial terminology—clarify expectations in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and sample sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may make sample editorial letters available only with client permission; sharing should respect client confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing a sample can help prospective clients understand an editor’s communication style, but lack of publicly available samples is not necessarily a red flag. Always confirm permissions and anonymize client details if samples are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other editing levels and their roles (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural editing: big-picture structure help. Content/substantive/editing: macro-to-micro blend of structural and line editing. Line editing/stylistic editing: clarity, tightness, flow. Copyediting: grammar, usage, spelling, punctuation. Proofreading: final word-by-word polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manuscript evaluation may touch on any of these if relevant to publishing/acceptance, but will not substitute for the deeper work each specialist performs. Choose the level of editing appropriate to the manuscript’s needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and caveats about standards and variability among editors
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universal standard definition for 'manuscript evaluation'—editors vary widely in depth, scope, and pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t get hung up on terminology; instead, interview multiple editors, request written proposals, and clarify exactly what will be delivered. Expect variation in practices and be skeptical of blanket statements claiming 'most' editors behave the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax and expense considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on how you file taxes, the expense of a manuscript evaluation (and other editing/publication expenses) may be deductible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check with your accountant for eligibility and record-keeping requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing rapport and protecting stylistic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should ensure an editor will respect their stylistic, ideological, linguistic, or aesthetic choices and that expectations are clearly stated and understood in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A free call and clear written agreement help establish trust and alignment. Discuss changes that are intentional stylistic choices (e.g., nonstandard first-person diction) so the editor knows what to preserve versus change.
